steps.title: Rías Baixas
steps.body: Rías Baixas, in Galicia, Spain's Atlantic north-west, is about 96% Albariño. It's named after the rías, flooded river valleys. Rainfall is high, 1,600 mm or more a year. Five sub-zones include Val do Salnés, coolest and most Atlantic, and O Rosal and Condado do Tea, warmer, along the Miño river. Granite soils dominate.

steps.title: Pergolas
steps.body: To fight humidity, vines are traditionally trained on high pergolas, called parras, on granite posts, two metres or more above the ground. Air circulates under the canopy, reducing rot; grapes stay away from damp soil. Some growers now use wire trellises, which allow more sun on the fruit.

steps.prompt: Match each Rías Baixas term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: Rías Baixas' landscape shapes its wine.

steps.title: Portugal
steps.body: Across the Miño, called Minho in Portugal, Albariño is called Alvarinho. It grows in Vinho Verde, especially in Monção e Melgaço. Spain and Portugal share the grape, divided by a river.

steps.prompt: Why are Albariño vines trained on high pergolas?
options: To let air circulate and reduce rot

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rías Baixas is about 96% Albariño on granite
Across the river, Portugal calls it Alvarinho
